To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

oxidative stress does not affect the gene expression of cholesterol transporters in endothelial cells, but it does induce the expression of adhesion molecules and MCP-1 in the presence of THP- 1 monocytes.

oxidative stress does not affect the gene expression of cholesterol transporters and nuclear receptors, but enhances the adhesion of THPs-1 monocytes and the expression of the adhesion molecules VCAM-1, MCP-1 and Eselectin in the presence of HUVECs.
iron/ascorbic acid induced oxidative stress in HUVEC does not affect cholesterol transport, but it enhances monocyte adhesion by upregulating ICAM-1 expression and downregulating eNOS mRNA.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a novel mechanism by which oxidative stress may contribute to atherogenesis, namely by enhancing the cellular adhesion between endothelial cells (ECs) and monocytes, which is associated with the downregulation of endothelial NO synthase (eNOS) and the upregulation of adhesion molecules.
the effects of oxidative stress on the expression of cholesterol transporters and the adhesion of monocytes to endothelial cells, which are both important processes in atherogenesis.
the role of oxidative stress in endothelial dysfunction and the initiation of atherogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

oxidative stress is a key player in the development of atherosclerosis and endothelial cell injury, and it can be considered as the first hit in the atherothrombogenic process, which may be further enhanced by the interaction between endothelial cells, monocytes and other cell types.

oxidative stress does not affect the expression status of the cholesterol transporters and nuclear receptors, but it does affect the gene expression of adhesion molecules, which in turn results in enhanced monocyte adhesiveness.
oxidative stress is not sufficient to induce the gene expression of cholesterol transporters in endothelial cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effect of oxidative stress in endothelial cells is not mediated via the regulation of the expression of the above mentioned molecules.

oxidative stress per se does not induce the gene expression of the investigated proteins, but it primes the cells for the subsequent adhesion of monocytes, thus promoting the inflammatory process in the vascular wall.
oxidative stress is able to modify the status of adhesion molecules, nuclear receptors and cholesterol transporters only in the presence of a second cell type.
The main takeaway from our work is that
oxidative stress may not be sufficient to induce the gene expression status required for cholesterol transport, but it may be able to enhance monocyte adhesion and endothelial cell activation.
oxidative stress is not a primary trigger for the initiation of atherosclerosis but rather a secondary effect of monocyte-endothelial cell interaction.
oxidative stress per se may not be the culprit in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis but it may act in a synergistic manner with other pro-atherogenic mediators.
